title: Appendix A — Proposal
text:
Reasons and Inspiration
Choosing between a cat and a dog is a common question for people who want a pet, and shelters with limited space and resources face it from the other side. We want to know whether one species is more likely to be adopted, and whether adoptions change with the seasons or from place to place. Answering these questions could help shelters decide where to focus adoption efforts.

title: Appendix A — Proposal
text:
Project Description
This project uses public animal shelter records to compare adoption outcomes for cats and dogs. We will look at how adoption rates differ by species and how they change across seasons and locations, using data wrangling and visualizations in R.

title: Appendix A — Proposal
text:
Research Questions

Are cats or dogs more likely to be adopted?
How do adoption rates change across months and seasons?
How do adoption rates vary by location (jurisdiction)?

title: Appendix A — Proposal
text:
Data Set
We will use the Long Beach Animal Shelter dataset from TidyTuesday (2025-03-04), originally from the City of Long Beach Animal Care Services. It has about 30,000 rows and 22 columns, and each row is one animal’s intake and outcome record. Useful variables include animal_type, outcome_type, intake_date, outcome_date, jurisdiction, latitude, and longitude. We will define the adoption rate as the share of a group’s outcomes that are adoptions.

title: Appendix B — Case Study
text:
How the story starts
Jan Diehm and Amber Thomas start with a problem that some jeans pockets are too small to hold everyday things. This gives readers a reason to care about the question the authors ask next: how much smaller are the pockets in women’s jeans? To find out, the authors measure pockets on 80 pairs of jeans from 20 brands.

title: Appendix B — Case Study
section: How the graphs tell the story
text:
How the graphs tell the story
The first graph shows the shape of each front pocket. As readers scroll, the graph highlights the average shape for men’s and women’s jeans. Showing the individual pockets first lets readers see how much they vary. The averages then make it easier to see that the pockets differ more in depth than in width.
In the next graph, readers can click on a phone, a wallet, or another item to see which pockets it fits in. This graph brings the story back to the problem at the start. Readers have already seen that women’s pockets are smaller. Now they can see how that difference affects what they can carry.

title: Appendix B — Case Study
text:
How the story ends
The authors then compare skinny and straight jeans. Women’s front pockets are smaller in both skinny and straight jeans. The difference between men’s and women’s jeans is much smaller for back pockets. At the end, the authors give a short history of pockets in women’s clothing and explain why it matters to be able to carry things and keep both hands free.

title: Appendix B — Case Study
text:
Source
Jan Diehm and Amber Thomas. “Women’s Pockets Are Inferior.” The Pudding, August 2018.
